title: The Secret Kingdom of Stefan George
author: Kyle Baasch
content:
![The Secret Kingdom of Stefan
George](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/IMG_4181-1.jpg)

Stefan George is the most elusive figure in the literary history of Wilhelmine
and Weimar Germany, a period that begins with Friedrich Nietzsche's
excoriations of Judeo-Christian morality in the late 1880s and ends with the
Nazi book burnings of 1933. From a distance, George's life looks like a secret
passageway connecting these two ominous termini. He appears as the Antichrist
in the age of democracy, as the counterrevolutionary herald of the Third
Reich.

The life of this poet is often divided into three periods. Around 1890, the
young George stood under the banner of "art for art's sake." He was inspired
by Mallarme and the French symbolists, with whom he studied in Paris; he later
translated Baudelaire's _Flowers of Evil_ into German. He established a
literary magazine that published his poems and those of his friends in small
limited editions for an invitation-only readership.

After 1900, in the second phase of his career, George metamorphosed from
Germany's leading exponent of aestheticism into a critic of enlightened
liberal-democratic culture: "a cold and disfigured humanity," as he called it
in a rare prose essay from 1907, "that boasts its manifold achievements while
great deeds and great love are vanishing." This "world of contradiction," he
wrote three years later, is "totally mechanical * totally shadowlike * totally
derivative and incapable of generating its own life." In 1913, George
published _Star of the Covenant_ , the holy scripture of George's emergent
brotherhood, in which a voice from heaven promises spiritual rebirth to his
devoted flock after the obliteration of the modern world: "Ten thousand men
must the holy madness smite / Ten thousand must the holy plague destroy / Tens
of thousands the holy war." The following year, German soldiers carried copies
of it into the trenches.

During the Weimar Republic, in the twilight of his career, George's poetic
activity receded. He devoted himself to mentorship, cultivating a cadre of
followers, often called the "George Circle," whose boyishly handsome members--
this was a selection criterion--were admired by Germany's intellectual
vanguard and appointed to prestigious academic posts at the best German
universities. They were celebrated for their monographs on great men among the
likes of Plato, Frederick II, and Napoleon, each thick volume bearing George's
trademark stamp of approval on its cover in the form of a curved swastika. It
is hardly surprising that some of George's followers trumpeted volkisch
ideology throughout the 1920s, or that a few remained committed to the Nazi
regime well after Hitler's rise to power in 1933--the year of George's death
in the Swiss village of Locarno at the age of sixty-five.

> "George was not a political theorist."

That is the shape of George's life in the imagination of someone who knows him
from sketches of modern German history, where his name sometimes appears
alongside those of illiberal political philosophers such as Oswald Spengler,
Carl Schmitt, and Ernst Junger. In the English-speaking world, where there has
never been much interest in George's poetry, this is where one is most likely
to encounter his message. This is unfortunate for several reasons. In the
first instance, George was not a political theorist; he was the most respected
German poet of his time. His name belongs in literary anthologies alongside
Rainer Maria Rilke and Thomas Mann, who were long considered lesser writers,
but whose posthumous fame overshadows George's work.

But even if one ignores George's poetry and sees him as he was seen in the
later years of his life, as the energetic prophet of _The New Reich_ --the
title of his final collection of poems--there is no clear path leading from
his aristocratic ethos to the racist mass movement that triumphed as he lay on
his deathbed. On the contrary, his work can be cited as a critique of Nazism,
and many of his disciples read it this way. The George Circle was a sanctuary
for Jewish intellectuals and homosexual poets in early twentieth-century
Germany, and even after 1933, these disciples never forsook the wisdom of
their "Master," as they called George with deference and affection. Almost all
of them carried his teaching into exile with unqualified devotion, nurturing
future generations of literary critics and historians in Princeton, Berkeley,
and Chapel Hill.

Despite this, for much of the past century, George has been regarded, at best,
as a sensitive lyric poet at home in _The Penguin Book of Homosexual Verse_ ,
and at worst, as a megalomaniacal cult leader and pedophile. But today it is
precisely those features of George's life long considered irredeemable--his
ethical severity and his cultivation of virtue in young men through the
educative power of love--that appear most inspiring and alive. At a time when
learning is becoming indistinguishable from vocational training, when the mind
confronts its technological obsolescence, and when the relations between
teachers and students are surveilled by Title IX officers, George appears,
with all his foibles, as an iconoclastic sage, man, and teacher.

* * *

The first thing one notices about George is the otherworldliness of his person
and work. He bore cartoonish features: a stumpy neck, usually obscured by a
high white shirt collar, supporting a spherical head with protuberant
cheekbones, thin lips, a protruding mandible, and deeply sunken eye sockets
that gave the impression of an insomniac. He wore a dense mane of hair swept
back, flowing perpendicular to his face as though a fan were pointed at his
nose.

> "He left his individual mark on all that he touched."

He was allergic to everything conventional that might restrict his will to
expression, and he left his individual mark on all that he touched. In his
poetry, he omitted articles, replaced semicolons and periods with a two-dot
ellipsis, and either forwent the comma or substituted a period centered like a
bullet point in its place. His signature was his use of lowercase letters for
nouns, which are necessarily capitalized in German so that they are not
mistaken for adjectives or verbs. These eccentricities, combined with archaic
diction, poetic contractions, and regional dialect, make it challenging to
read George's verse, which appears to be written in a private language.

The inaccessibility of George's poems was intensified by the psalmodic, anti-
theatrical intonation that George adopted when reading them. His idea of art
was negatively informed by commercial standards of evaluation. But to his
admirers--especially social philosophers like Georg Simmel, Georg Lukacs, and
Theodor Adorno--George's rigorous hermeticism was the source of his greatness.
He transcended the instrumental and degraded character of communicative
language by inventing a syntax in which humanity speaks as though for the
first time. It has still hardly been registered that the entire philosophical
critique of the "reification" of modern life did not begin with a rediscovery
of Hegel and Marx, but was born from a confrontation with George's longing for
a vital connection to his fellow men.

George also possessed an unconventional handwriting resembling the uncial
script used by the Christian scribes of late antiquity. His collaborator, the
graphic artist Melchior Lechter, helped design a special typeface on the basis
of this writing--today one can download the font under the name St-G-Schrift--
for George's poetry collections. The poems from the period of collaboration
with Lechter, which are usually considered George's finest, depict symbolic
dreamscapes that combine with art nouveau illustrations to form a kind of
_Gesamtkunstwerk_. _The Tapestry of Life_ (1900), for example, was published
on 17"x17" paper in an edition of 300, bound with wooden boards, and stylized
like a medieval incunabulum, with towering candelabra framing the poems.

This collection opens with a programmatic cycle in George's oeuvre: A world-
weary poet is confronted by his double in the form of a naked angel with
almond blossoms for fingers and a wreath of roses around his chin. The angel
says that he has been sent as a herald of "the beautiful life" before then
dropping a bouquet of lilies and mimosas onto the ground. As the poet bends to
retrieve the flowers, he is astonished to see the angel mirror his movement:
"Then HE too knelt * in bliss I bathed / My entire face in the fresh roses."
Ink drawings of angels, doves, harps, stars, and peacock feathers saturate
every corner of this exquisite and narcissistic erotic fantasy.

Something happened to George at the age of thirty-five, introducing a caesura
into his career with world-historical implications: He fell in love with a
thirteen-year-old boy. The Jewish scion, Maximilian Kronberger, had soft,
boyish features and a Mediterranean complexion. He wrote poetry that George
considered impressive. Most importantly, he showed George an admiration that
exceeded mere respect for his worldly experience and fame. Kronberger appeared
to George as the incarnation of "the beautiful life"--the realization of the
angel's message. Then, shortly before his sixteenth birthday, he died of
meningitis. And George became a teacher and prophet.

Heartbroken, George published a memorializing album of poems in honor of
"Maximin," as he renamed his beloved. A cropped image of Kronberger's head and
bare shoulders in profile appears adjacent to the title page of this extremely
rare book. (The original photograph, which extends down to the adolescent's
naked thighs, was hung on the walls of George's residences.) George prefaced
the album with a prose essay. He states that Maximin appeared in his midst as
"a plague seemed to rage that no medicine could help and that was to end in
the soullessness of the human race." But the boy "restored our confidence and
filled us with the light of new promises," for he embodied "almighty youth
just as we had dreamed it" and "he showed us things as they are seen by the
eyes of the Gods." He embodied a new value hierarchy oriented around youth,
male beauty, and creativity, such that "the oppressive present lost its
exclusive right since it had to submit to another order." Nietzsche called
this "the transvaluation of values."

George was neither the first to bemoan the soullessness of modern society nor
the first to dream of cultural renewal. These were pet themes of German
philosophy in the wake of Nietzsche. One famous meditation on this topic was
published the same year as Maximin's death: Max Weber's _The Protestant Ethic
and the Spirit of Capitalism_. This discipline-defining sociological study
concludes with a string of sentences that liken capitalist modernity to an
"iron cage" inhabited by the "Last Men" from Nietzsche's _Zarathustra_ :
maggot-men who think they have found happiness yet remain ignorant of their
own inconsequentiality, whom Weber calls "specialists without spirit,
sensualists without heart." Weber doubted that "new prophets" would arise to
vanquish the world of capitalist vocational culture with new values, but he
knew this was the only salvation.

Later in his career, Weber developed his trademark concept of "charisma" to
denote the logical possibility of a person who could challenge institutions
that had congealed into second nature. Charisma is a form of authority
grounded in the special "gift" of a divinely inspired individual, as opposed
to the authority of tradition or the rule of law. This obscure Pauline term
had never been applied to magnetic individuals until Weber adapted it for this
purpose. Incredibly, it has somewhat recently come to light that Weber's very
first printed use of this word--a word that, over the past century, has become
part of our everyday vocabulary--appears in a letter to a colleague about the
"utterly absurd" cult that George had erected around a dead teenager.

* * *

After the deification of Maximin, young people revered George as a divinely
inspired figure with the power to oppose modernity with an alternative vision.
He amassed disciples. Already, he was no stranger to mentorship. His frequent
collaborator Karl Wolfskehl, a colossal figure in Munich's fin-de-siecle
bohemian culture, had introduced him to his first disciple in 1899: Friedrich
Gundolf, a preposterously beautiful teenager then finishing his studies in
Darmstadt. Gundolf was George's first and proudest creation: a boundlessly
inventive mind formed entirely in George's mold, who would remain spiritually
devoted to his Master until his death in 1931.

Gundolf knew that his submission to George was alien to an individualistic
epoch for which autonomy is the highest value. In a 1908 essay on the subject
of "Allegiance and Discipleship," he criticizes the cult of "personality" as a
cloak for "talent without humanity * grandiloquence without need * brilliance
without body." The righteous man is not an autonomous individual; he
extinguishes his ego and "rejoices in making himself into fuel for a higher
flame." Another admirer of George, the young historian Friedrich Wolters,
ingratiated himself with George one year later with a similar essay on
"Lordship and Service," presenting a quasi-medieval social theory of
subjection under an all-powerful creative sovereign. George was impressed.

Gundolf was appointed to a position in Heidelberg in 1910, where he quickly
became the most beloved literature professor in Germany. Wolters began his
professorship in Marburg some years later. But they were both ruthless critics
of modern academic institutions, which poison the mind with abstractions and
weaken the faculty of valuation, the strength of convictions, while blocking
the appreciation of greatness in the world. This appears in the background of
Wolters's essay on servitude, which states that there is a "spiritual kingdom"
impervious to analytical observation with its own imperceptible atmosphere and
its own laws of transmission across generations.

The disclosure of these laws and the proclamation of what Wolfskehl called a
"Secret Germany" taking shape, under George's guidance, beneath the crumbling
Second Empire, was the impetus behind an antagonistic mock-academic anti-
journal co-edited by Gundolf and Wolters in 1910-11, called the _Yearbook for
the Spiritual Movement._ George contributed nothing but oversaw every aspect
of production. It is thus a fascinating glimpse into George's teaching; many
of the journal's themes would reappear in poeticized form in _Star of the
Covenant_ a few years later. A swastika appears on the title page of the
journal, which from this point forward--long before the symbol was
appropriated by the Nazis--is how George authorized his students' works.

> "George's idea of culture was influenced by the early Nietzsche."

A basic argument appears across the journal's three volumes: that the modern
secular notion of society as a decentralized system of semi-autonomous
functions run by atomized specialists is adversarial to culture as such.
George's idea of culture was influenced by the early Nietzsche, who had
defined it as "the unity of style in all the expressions of the life of a
people." The essence of culture lies "not in the diversity of its elements,"
writes one disciple, Berthold Vallentin, but in "the fusional power that gives
these elements form." Culture is nothing but coherence, and George felt that a
world pathologically driven by technological progress toward the intrinsically
limitless satisfaction of needs entails subordination to contradictory,
impersonal social structures while masquerading as the emancipation of
conscience, desire, and personality.

The most important contributions to the _Yearbook_ criticize the mechanistic
epistemological foundations of the modern sciences. Science, according to
Gundolf and Wolters, should enrich culture by harnessing the world's vital
forces in the direction of man's creative, form-giving power. But the basic
operation of modern science is the murderous re-conception of every seed of
spontaneous life as raw material for the satisfaction of the lowest human
desires. This implies the technological domination of nature and "the
despoliation of the forests," Gundolf notes. But even more insidiously, it
means the annihilation of the soul--the locus of life in the human being--
which is gnawed away by a corrosive intellectualism that allows rational
considerations to impede what would have been spontaneous moral decisions.
Ethical life, according to Gundolf, depends upon "the instinctive exclusion of
every restrictive and life-destroying element and the selective assimilation
of all that is conducive to life." But these instinctive actions appear to the
enlightened mind as arbitrary prejudices that must be dissolved by the acid of
reason.

The upshot of the mechanistic worldview is an atomistic theory of the
individual and a leveling spirit that spurns every deviation from uniform
mediocrity as a transgression against nature. Like Nietzsche, George believed
that the excellence of a culture is measured by the achievements of its
greatest specimens, not the living standards of its lowest. The combative
elitism of George's teaching flies in the face of liberal-democratic propriety
and is admittedly hard to read with much sympathy today. Gundolf was
contemptuous of "the masses" and felt that the average working-class citizen
was a rudderless bundle of drives calling out for a salutary yoke. Wolters--
who would soon come to represent a more aggressively political wing of the
George Circle--argues that if a nation declines from a lack of creative men,
"a neighboring nation with greater strength does right to dissolve this
degenerate entity and enslave what remains of it."

Moreover, for George and his disciples, it is always men who are the creative
ones, for "the power of woman can only be illuminated by the masculine flame."
The "disjointed, progressive, godless woman" of modernity, according to
Gundolf and Wolters, stands for ideals whose implementation will facilitate
"the extinction of all capable, powerful instincts in the face of pacifistic,
feminine, destructive ones." Wolters in particular regretted that childcare is
so often left in the hands of women, weakening the courage of young men. Women
are not teachers; learning is activated through an erotic tension between men
and boys.

* * *

Many of the intellectual women who had previously associated with George were
justly appalled by the _Yearbook_ 's misogyny and broke off all contact with
the Master. Others began to whisper that the George Circle was a pederastic
cult. Some combination of prudishness and morbid curiosity about George's
sexual proclivities, which today appear entirely at odds with the aggressive
antifeminism of his circle, has long stood in the way of a proper
understanding of the role of eros in George's orbit. We wonder: Was George
gay? Did he groom teenage boys? The compulsion to pathologize nonstandard
expressions of love did not quite exist in George's time as it does today. To
be sure, the figure of "the homosexual" had been around since the 1860s, and
George was often seen as one such figure. But it is important that George did
not use this word for himself.

George's attraction to boys was bound up with a pedagogical interest. All
education, he believed, is essentially erotic. "I am your proper teacher when
I love," he writes in _The New Reich_ , and "You are my proper pupil when you
love." A teacher who has never been aroused by the glow in the eye of his
student is not a real teacher, and a student who has never felt the urge to
gratify his teacher's erotic wishes has probably never learned anything. Men
copulate with women as a law of nature; men love boys as the ground of
culture. George had a word for this, which he used just once, in an
introduction to his virtuosic translation of Shakespeare's sonnets, which
Shakespeare for his part had addressed to a "Fair Youth." Recognizing that his
own epoch was bound to spurn or explain away the Bard's erotic fixation on a
nameless young man, George writes that "ages perverted by materialism and
intellectuality have no right to speak on this point, for they cannot even
imagine anything of the world-creating power of suprasexual love." What is
this?

George revered a kind of love that is neither asexual nor ignorant of the
body, but a sublimation of sexual desire that remains conscious of physical
beauty as its point of departure. Most of those accepted into his circle were
remarkably handsome young men, but for George this was only a facet of what
the Greeks called "kalokagathia." It indexed a harmonious constitution of the
soul. Eros that remains arrested at this level of animalistic arousal did not
interest George, regardless of whether it occurred between a man and a woman
or between two men. George was tolerant of sexual relations between men, which
were then criminalized under the German penal code, and some of his disciples
were open about their preference for men. But there is no evidence that he
granted his disciples anything more than affectionate handshakes and kisses on
the cheek. "Friendship between men must be educative and tragic," he once told
a disciple. "Otherwise, it is disgusting."

With a century of hindsight, it appears to us that George's idea of educative
homoeroticism was simply the repressed shape that gay love was forced to
assume at the time. But George's conviction was the opposite of this, and it
is worth taking seriously his idea that the modern notion of homosexuality--
the pathological conception that was fresh in George's time and is accepted as
a psychological identity in our own--obscures the essentially educative telos
of love between men.

Gundolf, who despite his love for George was an inveterate womanizer with no
homosexual inclinations, once suggested that George's erotic fascination with
young men was elucidated by Plato's _Symposium_ and _Phaedrus_ --George's two
favorite dialogues. "Only the Greeks and the Germans know world-creating
love," Gundolf writes in his book on George. This simplifies the matter too
much. George was stranger than Socrates. George wanted to breed a new German
nobility who resembled him in mien, gait, attitude, fashion. He wanted to
extricate young men from their corrupted middle-class households to establish
a new aristocratic race, a new dynasty.

> "Beauty was the surest sign of belonging to this dynasty."

Beauty was the surest sign of belonging to this dynasty, and it was necessary
for George to have the best stock. His disciples were thus stationed all over
Germany and were tasked with soliciting attractive boys on the streets, like
representatives of some dubious modeling agency scouting teens at a suburban
shopping mall in the 1990s. The disciples then described the boys in letters
to George and arranged initial interviews. This was a crucial, albeit bizarre,
component of George's "statecraft," the _Realpolitik_ of his spiritual
kingdom. Upon discovering that one such "miracle" had been living in
Heidelberg for years before being brought to his attention, George admonished
his disciples: "You just noticed this boy for the first time? Why do you even
have eyes?"

George's first meeting with his prospective disciples involved an exam. The
student had to read one of George's poems in the same rhythmic and liturgical
style that the Master was known for. In other ages, tests of intelligence and
physicality had been useful, but in the modern world, it is a young man's
intonation that betrays his chastity, his ability to withstand the pressures
of reality. But beyond the regular recitation of poetry, George did not have
any regimented educational program or cultish rituals, save the odd gathering
of his favorite disciples at Whitsuntide. He was foremost a spiritual mentor.
In the case of young students, he might administer handwriting exercises
(cursive betrays an impatient soul), assign poems to memorize, or discuss
whatever the student was studying in school. With older disciples, George
offered counsel on the form and content of their scholarly projects as much as
their marriage prospects. The goal in each case was neither the transmission
of knowledge nor the production of warriors, but the fortification of the
disciple's resistance to the conformist, world-destroying values of the middle
class.

The capstone for a disciple was to write a biography of a great man whose
harmonious soul and integral life--one in which every action is an unconscious
expression of the man's essence--could inspire a world that disfigures humans
into dead functionaries of abstract social systems. Conventional biographies
reduce a man to circumstances; the George Circle's biographies reduce these
circumstances to the formative agency of the creative man. Gundolf's _Goethe_
and Ernst Kantorowicz's _Frederick II_ are the two most famous examples. Like
all works of the George Circle, they were written in a vivid style, without
footnotes, and with clearly hagiographic, mythologizing intentions,
infuriating the established professoriate. And yet no one could deny that they
evidenced greater erudition than the unreadable studies of professional
academics. They presented the academy with a formidable opponent: humanistic
scholarship in the service of life.

* * *

Gundolf's closest friend, the Jewish historian and literary critic Erich
Kahler--who contributed an essay to the third volume of the _Yearbook_ and
occasionally hosted George at his Bavarian villa in the 1910s--expressed his
disappointment late in life, as an independent scholar living in Princeton,
that the George Circle had been repressed in Germany and that American
students did not even know the poet's name. "This is regrettable," he told an
audience in 1963, for "the life and work of this poet contain vital
instruction for our contemporary youth." For Kahler, George was a paragon of
"the power and impulse of self-mastery." He taught his followers to "hold fast
to the dignity of the human being in the whirlwind of world affairs."
Consequently, "in its innermost essence, the George Movement was diametrically
opposed to National Socialism."

This was an eccentric opinion in the 1960s and it remains one today. It would
require an entire book to tabulate the evidence for and against the George
Circle's complicity with Nazism. It is obvious from the _Yearbook_ that George
had illiberal and anti-democratic intentions for the future of Germany. In the
early months of World War I, Gundolf and Wolfskehl joined the chorus of pro-
war German intellectuals by writing enthusiastic articles for major news
outlets peppered**** with quotations from _Star of the Covenant_. They implied
that when George heralded the death of "tens of thousands in the holy war," he
authorized the sack of Belgium. But George did not share the war enthusiasm of
his contemporaries. When his disciples became overly concerned with politics,
he would chasten them by saying: "This has nothing to do with you."

Still, we might ask, why did he allow Wolters, who never quite espoused
George's "aesthetic fundamentalism," to abandon scholarship for nationalist
propaganda in the 1920s? And why did George permit Wolters's friends--who
dominated the circle after George's falling-out with Gundolf in the early
1920s--to promote racist and eugenicist ideas? And why did George feel, on the
eve of Hitler's rise to power, that the nation was starting to adopt his
views? On the other hand, why did George reject the Nazis' invitation to be an
honorary member of the Prussian Academy of Science in 1933, and why did he ask
one of his Jewish disciples to pen the response on his behalf? Most
interestingly, was the Nazi colonel Claus von Stauffenberg inspired by George,
his erstwhile mentor, when he attempted to assassinate Hitler in 1944? Why did
he shout, so it is rumored, "Long live Secret Germany," just before his
execution by firing squad?

The picture that emerges from these and a hundred other cases is one of an
aristocratic ethos that, in a moment of weakness, neglects the border
separating the spiritual kingdom from the real nation before then coming to
its senses and calling upon George's teaching in a moment of need.

The scholarly literature on George does not have a favorable opinion of his
teaching, though. The devotion he demanded from his disciples is said to have
prepared the nation to submit to a fascist dictator. But for George,
submission in the context of an erotic education is nothing at all like
submission in politics. The modern soul is sick, supple, and suggestible, and
George believed that its powers of resistance are paradoxically strengthened
by the authoritative grip of a teacher who can force it to find its inner
harmony. This explains why George's disciples often reported having felt
liberated under his authoritarian tutelage. By contrast, the autonomous agents
of the enlightened world, who refuse on principle to be led by another, "throw
themselves into the arms of the first bad man they see as soon as they are
brought to the point of despair," George once told a young disciple, "for they
do not have the courage to come to terms with life."

> "George scrutinized every word his students wrote."

In 1908, Gundolf wrote that "the concept of discipleship is alien and almost
ridiculous to our age." This is more so the case today. In the humanities,
where George left his mark on German learning, it is nonexistent. George
scrutinized every word his students wrote. He sat in on their university
lectures to ensure that they were taking seriously their task as ambassadors
of higher culture. And these disciples were deadly serious, for they revered
George and did not want him to withdraw his love. By contrast, the ideal-
typical relationship between teachers and students today is transactional and
businesslike. It is common, for example, for graduate advisors to pass a
dissertation without having read a word of it, to encourage early career
scholars to neglect their teaching in favor of high-impact scholarship that no
one will ever read, and to shrug their shoulders as the art and thinking and
the craft of writing are rendered irrelevant by LLMs.

There are many good reasons to disagree with George's anti-democratic
aspirations, to scrutinize his method of acquiring disciples, and to impeach
his moral probity at the dawn of the Third Reich. He is not the right teacher
for our present moment. But in a world without teachers, it is worth returning
to the life of the Master to recall what such a figure once was.
